description.value: This fMRI study examined neural correlates of attentional bias to high-, low-energy food and neutral images in restrained and unrestrained eaters.

spans.text: Thus, functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) was conducted in individuals (12 restraint eaters, 12 unrestraint eaters) exposed to high/low-energy food and neutral images while performing a two-choice oddball task.

value: we hypothesized that restrained eaters would show hyper-responsivity in the brain regions associated with food reward.
we concluded that restrained eaters may exhibit elevated responsivity of brain attention circuitry to food cues.

Because the standard stimulus is presented much more frequently than the deviants, the detection of task-relevant infrequent events (such as high energy-food or cigarette cues) for obese people and active smokers has been associated with a faster P300 latency in event-related potentials (ERP) and a blood oxygenation level-dependent (BOLD) response in the frontal cortex and occipital-temporal regions, representing greater attentional processing for the deviant stimuli .
subjects are instructed to make a standard/deviant distinction by pressing different keys

instructions.value: Make a standard/deviant distinction by pressing different keys as accurately and rapidly as possible; press one key for standard stimuli and the other for deviant stimuli. Participants were told the purpose was to investigate fast response selection and inhibition of the prepotent response to the frequent picture when a deviant appeared.

spans.text: Prior to the experiment, all subjects were told that the purpose of the study was to investigate their ability to make a fast response selection and their ability to inhibit the prepotent response to the frequent picture when the deviant appeared.

stimuli.value: A frequent standard picture of a cup and deviant pictures grouped into high-energy food, low-energy food, and neutral categories. Each block contained one deviant category; images were presented for 800 ms.

spans.text: The frequent standard stimulus was a picture of a cup, and the deviants were 30 pictures grouped as either high-energy food (e.g., cake, pizza, hamburger, ice cream), low-energy food (e.g., vegetables, fruits), or neutral (e.g., flower, light bulb).
The false responses and responses exceeding the time limit were rare, as nearly all subjects achieved more than 97% accuracy rates in this experiment.
